title.en: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
The dignity of every kind of work

text.en: Think of everyone whose work you used today: the person who made your shoes, the electrician who keeps the lights on, the cook who made lunch. This poem listens to all of them celebrating together.

Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations is an anonymous poem. The speaker hears Bharat celebrating the many vocations of its people.
The poem names craftspeople, artisans with lutes, carpenters, electricians, boatmen, shoemakers, a cook, a designer and a mason, so it gives us a whole community at work.
Each worker gets one vivid detail: carpenters work with mathematical precision, electricians bring light with wires, and boatmen return with stories of the sea.
The poem uses auditory imagery, language that appeals to hearing, with words such as hear, humming, singing and rhythm. We seem to hear the work.
Shoemakers affirm the quality of their work for the feet that walk, dance, run and jump. The poem shows that humble work supports everything we do.
The poem begins and ends with the speaker hearing Bharat celebrating the varied voices. This framing gives it a feeling of completeness.
The last lines say that the voice of a vocation is the voice of a person's identity. What we do is a part of who we are.
The poem does not follow a strict rhyme scheme, so it is free verse. Its theme is the dignity of labour and respect for every vocation.

problem.en: Explain why the poet says the voice of a vocation is the voice of identity.

text.en: Each worker is proud of the skill that belongs to them.

why.en: Look at celebrating what belongs to them.

text.en: A person's work shapes how they are known.
So respecting work means respecting the person.

prompt.en: Why does the poet list so many different vocations?

requiredIdeas.en: To show every kind of work has value
Auditory imagery lets us hear the work

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking only skilled or famous jobs are celebrated

points.en: The poem is an anonymous celebration of the varied vocations of Bharat.
Auditory imagery lets the reader hear the work.
The poem begins and ends with the same idea and has no strict rhyme scheme.
Its theme is the dignity of labour and identity through work.
